title: Conversable Quantum Fire in the Standard Model
authors: Ofer Casper, Barak Nehoran, Or Sattath
abstract: Quantum fire consists of quantum states that can be efficiently functionally cloned but cannot be transmitted using one-way classical communication. Whereas all previous quantum-fire constructions with proven untelegraphability are relative to an oracle, ours, based on one-shot signatures, is in the standard model.   Our construction achieves two further notions that we introduce: (a) keyless untelegraphability, a strengthening of untelegraphability; and (b) conversability, meaning that a flame, though not telegraphable via one-way classical communication, can be transmitted via classical interaction. Hence one-way and two-way classical communication differ qualitatively in their power to transmit this quantum fire.   We use these two novel properties of quantum fire, along with its clonability, to give one of the first cryptographic applications of quantum fire. Keyless untelegraphability forces the distribution of serial numbers of valid flames to have high min-entropy, while conversability and clonability allow the corresponding flame to be cloned and transferred using only classical communication.   We present two variants of our conversable quantum-fire construction. The first, based on one-shot signatures (instantiable from subexponential iO, subexponentially secure one-way functions, and LWE), supports polynomially many flames, and super-logarithmic min-entropy of the serial-number distribution. The second, under the stronger assumption of exponentially unforgeable one-shot signatures (instantiable relative to a classical oracle), supports exponentially many flames, and linear min-entropy.
summary: This paper introduces "conversable quantum fire," a quantum state that can be copied but not classically transmitted in one direction. By leveraging this primitive, the authors construct a novel, classically verifiable scheme for certifying high min-entropy, demonstrating a deep link between quantum information theory and modern cryptography.
main_problem: The paper aims to construct a quantum primitive called "quantum fire" that is clonable but untelegraphable, and to establish its cryptographic utility for certifying min-entropy.
main_result: The authors prove the existence of a publicly certifiable, classically transferable min-entropy scheme based on a "conversable quantum fire" construction derived from one-shot signatures.
method: The construction utilizes novel properties—keyless untelegraphability and conversability—to link quantum information security to classical cryptographic primitives like one-shot signatures.
model_or_system: The model centers on quantum states exhibiting "quantum fire" properties, which are constructed using one-shot signatures, LWE, and are analyzed through protocols involving cloning, verification, and classical interaction.
key_observables: Clonability, untelegraphability, keyless untelegraphability, conversability, and the resulting min-entropy of the serial number distribution.
important_parameters: The construction has two variants: one supporting polynomially many flames (logarithmic depth) and another supporting exponentially many flames (linear depth).
main_assumptions: The constructions rely on the existence of unforgeable one-shot signatures and the ability to perform classical interactions (conversability).
figures_summary: The figures graphically define the syntax and security games for one-shot signatures and quantum fire, illustrating the processes of sparking, cloning, verifying, and conversing a quantum flame.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by defining the primitives (one-shot signatures, quantum fire) graphically, proving the novel properties (keyless untelegraphability, conversability), and culminating in the construction of the classically certifiable min-entropy scheme.
why_interesting: While highly theoretical, the concepts of quantum state transferability and information security are foundational to quantum computation and quantum networking protocols, providing rigorous bounds on classical communication capabilities.
